question.text: What happens to option Greeks near expiry for an ATM option?

answer.text: Delta approaches 0.5, Gamma becomes very large (delta changes rapidly), Theta becomes very negative (rapid time decay), and Vega decreases (less time for volatility to matter)
All Greeks approach zero near expiry
Delta approaches 1, Gamma approaches 0, Theta approaches 0
All Greeks remain constant throughout the option's life

explanation.text: The Logic: For an at-the-money option near expiry, delta sits in the neighborhood of 0.5 because the outcome is highly uncertain — a small move can flip the option from OTM to ITM and back. That uncertainty translates into a very high gamma (delta is changing rapidly with the underlying), and a very negative theta (the remaining time value is being eroded rapidly with very little time left). Vega falls because, with little time remaining, even a change in volatility has less room to affect the premium. The Trap: The Greeks of a near-expiry ATM option do not all collapse to zero, and ATM delta does not approach 1 (it stays roughly at 0.5). Greeks are not constant — they change materially with moneyness, time, and volatility. Note: The NISM Series I (Currency Derivatives) and Series IV (Interest Rate Derivatives) workbook pages reviewed define delta, gamma, theta and vega and note that vega is lower when less time remains, but the combined near-expiry ATM picture — gamma spike, sharply negative theta, and delta near 0.5 — was not located together in the workbook pages reviewed. The framing above is presented as general option-Greeks industry knowledge rather than a workbook citation.
